final_answer:
Short answer: the husband's practical path is to (1) file, with the immigration court, a motion to reopen and rescind the August 1, 2025 in absentia removal order based on lack of notice under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) (8 U.S.C. 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii); 8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii)), and (2) if reopened, pursue adjustment of status before the immigration judge, while separately addressing the I-130 with USCIS. Nothing can be done productively about the USCIS denials first, because once he is in removal proceedings the IJ, not USCIS, has jurisdiction over his I-485.

1. Immigration court filing. An in absentia order may be rescinded on a motion to reopen filed at any time upon a showing that the alien did not receive notice under INA 239(a)(1) or (2). Here the NTA went to an address the couple never gave, so the facts fit the lack-of-notice ground, subject to proof. There is no 180-day limit for this ground (the 180-day limit applies only to the exceptional-circumstances ground, 240(b)(5)(C)(i)); filing on or after April 1, 2026 is therefore timely. Filing the motion automatically stays removal pending the IJ's decision. Practical contents: a written motion to the immigration court that issued the order, with a sworn declaration from the husband (and wife) that no NTA or hearing notice was received and the address was never provided, proof of the address actually given to USCIS (I-130/I-485 receipt notices, I-485 and I-130 forms), evidence of diligence (they believed USCIS cases were pending; prompt action upon learning of the order), the NTA/hearing notice showing the wrong address, and a request to rescind the order and terminate or continue proceedings. A copy of the application for relief (here, a renewed I-485 with supporting I-130 evidence) should accompany the motion where possible. Also file a change of address (EOIR-33) and, if represented, an EOIR-28. Under Matter of M-R-A-, 24 I&N Dec. 665 (BIA 2008), regular-mail delivery is only a weaker presumption; but that presumption attaches to notices sent to the address the alien provided, and the husband should offer affidavits, diligence evidence and the fact that he had applied for relief (incentive to appear). Caution: Campos-Chaves v. Garland, 602 U.S. 447 (2024), holds that an alien who actually receives a proper 239(a)(2) notice of hearing cannot use (C)(ii) merely because the NTA was defective; it does not help if notice was never received, which is this husband's claim. If the IJ finds notice was properly sent to the address of record and denies, the alternative (C)(i) exceptional-circumstances ground is time-barred (180 days), and discretionary/sua sponte reopening or BIA appeal (30 days from IJ denial) would be the remaining routes.

2. Fees. As I found, the EOIR motion-to-reopen fee for an IJ is $1,065 for FY2026 ($145 plus the $920 OBBBA fee), but the fee does not apply to a motion to reopen an in absentia order filed under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii). So the lack-of-notice motion carries no filing fee. If the IJ reopens, the renewed I-485 filed in proceedings is filed with the court with the applicable fees (EOIR/DHS fee rules for I-485 in proceedings; I did not verify the amounts, and the I-485 fee and biometrics are paid to DHS). If the motion were instead characterized as exceptional-circumstances, the fee would apply; a fee waiver request is possible if unable to pay. Not verified from primary text: I could not access the eCFR/Federal Register directly, so the fee statements rest on secondary summaries of the Federal Register notices and EOIR guidance.

3. Contesting the I-130/I-485 denials. USCIS denials: a motion to reopen/reconsider on Form I-290B is due within 30 days (8 CFR 103.5(a)(1)(i)); an untimely motion may be excused in USCIS's discretion if the delay was reasonable and beyond the applicant's control, which the wrong-address mailing supports, but the proceedings in court change the analysis: with an NTA filed, 8 CFR 1245.2(a)(1) gives the IJ exclusive jurisdiction over the I-485 for non-arriving aliens, so the I-485 should be renewed before the IJ after reopening (the IJ can also assess bona fides of the marriage). The I-130 remains USCIS's to adjudicate (the IJ cannot approve an I-130), so file a late I-290B (or, if safer, a new I-130 with the wife as petitioner) and ask the IJ to continue the case. Where a denial was for failure to respond to an RFE, abandonment-denial evidentiary rules in 8 CFR 103.5(a)(2) apply. Because the RFE was mailed to an unprovided address, show proof of address of record.

4. Merits risks. As an immediate relative who was inspected and admitted on a B-2, he may be eligible under INA 245(a) and (c) exceptions for immediate relatives, but the marriage 19 days after entry on a B-2 and I-485 filing within weeks raises a willful-misrepresentation/preconceived-intent risk (INA 212(a)(6)(C)(i); State Department 90-day rule as a guide), plus the overstay is forgiven for immediate relatives. I did not research this in depth.

Unresolved: whether the IJ will credit non-receipt; I could not independently verify certain regulatory text or very recent BIA developments (a search result mentioned a 2026 BIA decision, Matter of Diji, on notices, which I did not review).
